column2: Banks can transform short-term deposits into longer-term loans, providing intermediation while exposing themselves to liquidity and maturity-mismatch risks.
column3: Deposit-funded long-term lending removes maturity mismatch because both deposits and loans appear on the same balance sheet.

column2: A solvent bank can face a liquidity shortfall if near-term withdrawals exceed available cash and funding; positive net worth alone does not settle the timing problem.
column3: Positive net worth guarantees that every immediate withdrawal can be paid without obtaining liquidity.

column2: Borrower default is credit risk, while a trading bond's loss from an interest-rate change is market risk; both can affect the same institution through different channels.
column3: A trading bond's interest-rate loss is borrower default risk even when the borrower pays every contractual amount.

column2: Loss from an internal processing failure can be operational risk, distinct from a deliberate change in a borrower's credit quality or a quoted market price.
column3: A payment-processing failure is market risk because its resulting loss is expressed in money.

column2: For otherwise comparable fixed-rate bonds, rising required yields lower market prices; longer duration generally gives greater price sensitivity to a small yield change.
column3: Rising required yields increase existing fixed-rate bond prices because future interest receipts become more valuable.

column2: Eligible regulatory capital 12 and risk-weighted assets 100 imply a 12% ratio; increasing RWA to 120 with capital unchanged reduces it to 10%.
column3: That ratio remains 12% after RWA rises to 120 because nominal capital has not changed.

column2: Basel III distinguishes common equity Tier 1, additional Tier 1 and Tier 2; equal nominal rupee amounts in different instruments need not have identical eligibility or loss-absorption quality.
column3: Every bank-issued borrowing instrument automatically qualifies as common equity Tier 1 because it supplies funding.

column2: A leverage-ratio measure uses an exposure measure without the same credit-risk weights as the risk-based capital ratio, providing a complementary constraint.
column3: A leverage ratio and a risk-weighted capital ratio are numerically identical whenever they use the same capital amount.

column2: LCR addresses a specified short-term liquidity stress horizon, while NSFR addresses stable funding over a longer structural horizon; one measure does not substitute mechanically for the other.
column3: A satisfactory short-term LCR proves adequate structural stable funding without assessing assets' funding requirements.

column2: Under applicable prudential rules, overdue status can trigger asset classification even when collateral appears valuable; security value alone does not justify ignoring recognition requirements.
column3: A fully secured overdue loan cannot become non-performing because collateral substitutes for payment performance.

column2: Recognising a loan-loss provision and writing off an exposure are distinct accounting actions; a provision does not by itself extinguish the borrower's legal debt.
column3: Creating a provision automatically releases the borrower from repayment of the same amount.

column2: Net NPA adjusts gross NPA for specified provisions and related adjustments; a lower net figure can reflect provisioning rather than fewer newly defaulting loans.
column3: A fall in net NPA necessarily proves a matching fall in fresh defaults even if provisioning increased.

column2: Cash reserve requirements and prescribed holdings of eligible liquid assets are different instruments; government securities do not automatically substitute for every required cash balance.
column3: Holding additional government securities automatically meets an equal amount of every cash reserve requirement.

column2: A collateralised repo is a financing transaction with reversal terms, while an outright open-market purchase changes securities holdings through a purchase; both can affect liquidity differently.
column3: An outright purchase and a repo are identical because neither creates a future reversal obligation.

column2: A policy change can pass imperfectly to lending rates when funding mix, credit risk or bank conditions change; observed loan pricing is not determined by the policy rate alone.
column3: Unchanged policy rates require unchanged lending rates even if borrower risk and bank funding costs rise.

column2: Treasury bills are ordinarily money-market instruments, while long-term bonds are capital-market instruments; issuer identity alone does not determine the maturity classification.
column3: Every government-issued security is a money-market instrument regardless of its original maturity.

column2: New share issuance transfers funds to the issuer through the primary market; trading existing shares mainly transfers ownership and funds between investors in the secondary market.
column3: An investor's ordinary purchase of existing shares directly finances the issuer by the full transaction price.

column2: Banks and NBFCs have different regulatory permissions and functions; an NBFC does not acquire every bank privilege merely by offering loans.
column3: Any licensed NBFC can perform every demand-deposit and payment-system function of a bank because both are financial intermediaries.

column2: Long-gestation development projects may need financing suited to their cash-flow profile; a development-finance role differs from simply maximising short-term deposit turnover.
column3: Development finance is defined solely by collecting short-term household deposits and requires avoiding long-gestation projects.

column2: Fund assets Rs 110, liabilities Rs 10 and 10 units imply NAV Rs 10 per unit; NAV is based on net assets rather than gross holdings alone.
column3: Those figures imply NAV Rs 11 because fund liabilities are ignored in investors' unit value.

column2: An income distribution can reduce a fund's ex-distribution NAV, other things equal; the distribution plus remaining NAV must be considered before inferring investment loss.
column3: An NAV fall equal to a cash distribution proves an investor lost that amount even when the distribution was received.

column2: A diversified equity fund can reduce concentration risk but remains exposed to market risk; a collective investment wrapper does not guarantee capital protection.
column3: Collective ownership through a mutual fund makes an equity portfolio's principal guaranteed without any separate guarantee.

column2: An opened but persistently unused account does not by itself establish effective inclusion; accessible payments, savings, credit and suitable service use also matter.
column3: The number of accounts opened alone establishes successful sustained financial inclusion irrespective of access and usage.

column2: Digital payment convenience does not eliminate authentication or operational risk; stronger verification can address particular threats without guaranteeing zero fraud.
column3: Introducing two-factor authentication eliminates all fraud, including authorised payments induced by deception.

column2: Insurable interest and indemnity address different aspects of insurance; ordinary property indemnity aims to compensate covered loss rather than provide unlimited gain.
column3: Insurable interest permits a property insured to claim any sum above the covered loss because the relationship itself determines unlimited compensation.

column2: A life policy's agreed benefit is distinguished from ordinary property indemnity based on measured financial loss; treating all insurance as identical strict indemnity is inaccurate.
column3: Every life-policy payment must equal proved replacement cost under the same strict property-indemnity computation.

column2: Material risk information affects underwriting; an omission can be material even when it has no relation to the premium the applicant personally hoped to pay.
column3: Information is material only if the applicant agrees that it should increase the premium.

column2: After an indemnity insurer pays a covered loss, subrogation can transfer relevant recovery rights to the insurer to prevent double recovery, subject to applicable terms and law.
column3: Subrogation entitles the insured to retain full indemnity and a second full recovery for the identical loss without adjustment.

column2: Riskier applicants disproportionately seeking cover illustrates adverse selection; reduced care after obtaining cover illustrates moral hazard.
column3: Reduced care after purchasing insurance is adverse selection because it concerns selection after the policy begins.

column2: Reinsurance transfers specified insurer risk to a reinsurer under a separate arrangement; it does not automatically remove the original insurer's obligations to its policyholder.
column3: Reinsurance automatically substitutes the reinsurer as the policyholder's only contractual insurer and releases the original insurer.
